Output? t.run(); t.start(); t.join(); t.start(); where the task prints the thread name and t is named "worker".

main
worker
java.lang.IllegalThreadStateException   (thrown by the second start)
Verified. run() is an ordinary call on the main thread. start() launches the new thread, and join() makes the order fixed. A second start() throws, because a thread can never be restarted, and the state stays TERMINATED.
Output? Current thread interrupts itself, then prints isInterrupted() twice and Thread.interrupted() twice.

Thread.currentThread().interrupt();
System.out.println(Thread.currentThread().isInterrupted());   // true
System.out.println(Thread.currentThread().isInterrupted());   // true
System.out.println(Thread.interrupted());                     // true, and clears the flag
System.out.println(Thread.interrupted());                     // false
Verified. isInterrupted() only reads the flag. The static Thread.interrupted() reads and clears it.
A sleeping thread is interrupted. What is the flag inside the catch block? What if the flag was set before sleep() was called?

Inside catch (InterruptedException e), isInterrupted() returns false, because throwing the exception clears the flag (verified). That's why you must restore it with Thread.currentThread().interrupt() if you don't rethrow.
If the flag is already set when sleep is called, it throws immediately without sleeping, with the message sleep interrupted (verified).
Why are wait(), notify() and notifyAll() on Object and not on Thread?

Because a thread waits on a condition guarded by a lock, and in Java any object can be that lock. The wait set belongs to the monitor, and the monitor belongs to the object. A thread doesn't wait for a particular other thread. If these methods were on Thread, one thread would need to know which thread to signal, and any object couldn't serve as a coordination point.
Compare sleep, wait, join, yield and LockSupport.park.

Method | Releases locks? | Needs monitor? | Woken by
Thread.sleep | No | No | Timeout, interrupt
Object.wait | Only that one monitor | Yes | notify, timeout, interrupt, spuriously
Thread.join | No locks of the caller, except the Thread object's monitor internally | No | Target ends, timeout, interrupt
Thread.yield | No | No | Only a hint, may continue at once
LockSupport.park | No | No | unpark, interrupt (no exception), spuriously
wait only releases the monitor it's called on. Other monitors the thread holds stay held, which is a source of deadlocks with nested locks. unpark grants a single permit, so an unpark before park isn't lost, unlike a notify with no waiter.
A worker thread throws an unchecked exception. What happens to main?

Nothing. Only that thread dies. The exception doesn't propagate across threads. The handler is called with the thread and exception, and main carries on. In a test with a handler that printed a message, the output was bad died: boom and then main still alive. try/catch around t.start() in the parent can't catch it, because the exception happens in a different stack.
When does the JVM exit? What happens if main ends while other threads run?

The JVM exits when all non-daemon threads have finished, or when System.exit or Runtime.halt is called, or on a fatal signal or crash. If main ends while non-daemon threads run, the JVM stays up. main isn't special. Daemon threads are abandoned at exit, without running their finally blocks. Shutdown hooks run on normal exit and on System.exit, but not on halt or kill -9.
What happens when you call obj.wait() or notify() outside synchronized?

Both compile, then throw java.lang.IllegalMonitorStateException: current thread is not owner at runtime (verified). The compiler can't know which monitor you hold. The rule exists to prevent lost wakeups: the condition check and the sleep must be one atomic step, which only the lock gives you.
Can two threads run two different synchronized methods of the same object? What about static and instance?

- Two synchronized instance methods on the same object: no, they share this.
- The same methods on different objects: yes, different locks.
- A synchronized method and a non-synchronized one: yes. synchronized only excludes others that use the same lock.
- A static synchronized and an instance synchronized method: yes. One locks the Class object and the other locks the instance. If both touch a static field, that's a race.
What does this print? volatile int c; with two threads each doing c++ a million times.

The output is not deterministic. It's usually less than 2,000,000. c++ is a read, an add and a write. volatile makes each read and write visible but doesn't join them into one step, so two threads can read the same value and lose an update. Fix with AtomicInteger, LongAdder or a lock.
Which Thread.State is a thread in when it waits for a ReentrantLock? For a socket read? After notify()?

- Waiting on ReentrantLock.lock(): WAITING (or TIMED_WAITING for a timed tryLock), because it parks. BLOCKED is reserved for monitors.
- Blocked in a socket read: RUNNABLE. The JVM doesn't track blocking in native code as a state, so a thread hung on a dead connection looks "running" in a dump.
- After notify(): BLOCKED until the notifier releases the monitor, then RUNNABLE. Tested on Java 21: WAITING before notify, BLOCKED while main still held the lock.
Why was Thread.stop() removed from use? What replaces it?

stop() threw an asynchronous ThreadDeath at any point in the target's code, which released all its monitors immediately. Objects those monitors protected could be left half-updated, visible to everyone, with no error shown. It was deprecated in Java 1.2 and has thrown UnsupportedOperationException since Java 20. The replacement is interruption, or a volatile flag, where the target stops at a safe point of its own choosing.
Are local variables thread-safe? Is an object referenced by a local variable?

Local primitives and references live on the thread's own stack, so they can't be shared. The object a local refers to is on the heap, and it's confined only if the reference never escapes. If you pass it to another thread, store it in a field or return it to shared code, it's shared. A lambda capturing a local AtomicInteger and running on several threads shares that object, even though the variable is local.
Is a Spring singleton bean thread-safe?
Why does double-checked locking need volatile? Was it always safe with volatile?

Publishing the reference can be reordered with the constructor's writes, so without volatile, the unsynchronized first check can see a non-null reference to an uninitialized object. Volatile adds a happens-before edge from the write to every later read. Before Java 5, it was broken even with volatile, because the old memory model didn't stop ordinary writes moving past volatile ones. JSR-133 in Java 5 fixed that.
Explain happens-before. If A happens-before B, must A run earlier in real time?

Happens-before is a guarantee about visibility: if A happens-before B, then B sees A's effects. It's a partial order built from rules such as program order, monitor unlock to lock, volatile write to read, thread start and join, combined by transitivity.
It doesn't say that A physically executes earlier. The JVM may reorder two statements in the same thread if no one can observe the difference. The reverse also fails: A running earlier in real time, with no happens-before relation, gives no guarantee that B sees A's write.
What can this print? int data; boolean ready; Writer: data = 42; ready = true; Reader: while (!ready); print(data);

The behaviour is not deterministic, since it's a data race. Three outcomes are allowed: it prints 42, it prints 0 (the writes appeared reordered), or it never terminates, because the JIT may hoist ready out of the loop. Making ready volatile guarantees 42 by the chain shown in the happens-before diagram.
Does final make an object thread-safe?

Only partly. A final field guarantees that the reference is set and visible after construction, along with what was reachable through it at that time. It doesn't make the referenced object immutable. final List<String> names = new ArrayList<>() is a fixed reference to a mutable, unsynchronized list. Elements added after construction get no guarantee at all. The class needs all state final and no mutation after construction, and this must not escape during it.
Is iterating a Collections.synchronizedList safe? What's a thread-safe way to do check-then-act on a map?
What is CAS and what are its downsides?

CAS atomically stores a new value only if the location still holds the expected value. Retry loops built on it give lock-free counters and data structures. Threads never block, so there's no deadlock, and a stalled thread can't hold up others.
Downsides:
- Under heavy contention, repeated failures waste CPU and cause cache-line traffic.
- The ABA problem.
- It covers one variable. Several variables must be combined into one immutable object behind an AtomicReference.
- The update function may run several times, so it must have no side effects.
Output? new AtomicReference<Integer>(100).compareAndSet(100, 101), then the same with 1000 and 1001.

Prints true, then false (verified). AtomicReference compares references. 100 is boxed from the Integer cache, so both boxes are the same object. 1000 is outside the default cache range, so the two boxes differ. Use AtomicInteger for numbers, or keep the exact reference you got from get().
AtomicLong vs LongAdder: which and when?

Use LongAdder for write-heavy statistics under contention, such as request counters. It spreads updates across cells, so threads don't fight over one location. sum() is not a consistent snapshot, and it doesn't return a value on increment.
Use AtomicLong when each update's result matters: ID generation, or CAS decisions like "only increment if below the limit". With low contention, the two perform about the same and AtomicLong uses less memory.
synchronized or ReentrantLock in new code? Why does lock() go before try?

Default to synchronized when it's enough: it's shorter, and you can't forget to release it. Choose ReentrantLock when you need a timeout, interruptible waiting, several conditions, fairness or queue inspection. On Java 21 to 23 only, avoid long blocking inside synchronized with virtual threads, because of pinning.
lock() goes just before try. If it were inside and threw, finally would call unlock() without the lock being held, and that IllegalMonitorStateException would hide the original error.
What's the difference between fair and non-fair locks? Why is non-fair the default?

Fair locks grant access in roughly arrival order. Non-fair locks let an arriving thread take a free lock at once, jumping the queue. Waking a parked thread takes a long time compared with a short critical section. A running thread that barges in and gets out again can complete inside that gap, so non-fair throughput is much better. The risk is that some threads wait a long time. Use fairness only when bounded waiting truly matters, and note that it doesn't guarantee fair OS scheduling.
Output? A thread holding a read lock calls writeLock().tryLock(). Then a thread holding the write lock calls readLock().tryLock().

The first returns false and the second true (verified). Upgrading isn't supported: read holders block writers, including yourself. With plain lock() it would hang forever. Downgrading works, because a writer is exclusive and can safely also take a read lock. After unlocking the write lock, the read count remained 1.
When would you use StampedLock? What are its traps?

Use it for read-mostly data with short reads, where ReentrantReadWriteLock overhead shows up. An optimistic read writes no shared state, so readers scale, and writers aren't blocked by them.
Traps:
- Not reentrant, so nested acquires deadlock. On a held write lock, tryWriteLock() and tryReadLock() returned 0 when tested.
- In an optimistic section you must copy to locals, then validate, and only then use the values. Data read before validation can be inconsistent, so don't follow pointers or index arrays based on it.
- No Conditions, and stamps must be matched to the right unlock method.
Is a Semaphore with one permit the same as a mutex? Output of new Semaphore(1) then release() then availablePermits()?

Prints 2 (verified): permits are just a count, and release doesn't check that you acquired one.
It's not the same as a mutex. A semaphore has no owner, so any thread can release it. It isn't reentrant, so a second acquire by the same thread blocks. That lack of ownership is a feature in signalling between threads, but a mistake in a finally can silently add permits and weaken your limit.
CountDownLatch vs CyclicBarrier vs Phaser?

- CountDownLatch: one-shot. Waiters wait for N events, which anyone can signal, and the waiters don't have to be the signallers. After zero it's permanently open.
- CyclicBarrier: reusable. N threads wait for each other, with an optional action when they all arrive. A failure breaks it for everyone.
- Phaser: a flexible barrier. Parties can register and leave between phases, phases are numbered, and it can be tiered for large groups. When the last party deregisters, it terminates.
Explain the ThreadLocal memory leak. Why is the key weak if the value still leaks?

Values live in a map on the Thread, with a weak reference to the ThreadLocal key and a strong reference to the value. In a pool the thread lives on, so the value lives on until it's removed.
A weak key is a partial defence. If the map held the key strongly, a dropped ThreadLocal could never be collected, as long as the thread lived. With a weak key, the ThreadLocal can be collected, the entry becomes stale, and later get, set and rehash operations can clear stale entries. That cleanup is opportunistic, and it doesn't happen at all if nobody touches the map. So always call remove() in finally.
Output? On a single-thread executor, task 1 sets a ThreadLocal to "alice", and task 2 reads it.

Prints alice (verified). Both tasks ran on the same reused thread, and the value was never removed. In production this leaks one user's context into another's request, which is a security bug and not only a memory one.
What is ScopedValue? Is it final? How does it compare to ThreadLocal?

A way to share an immutable value with everything called within a bounded scope: ScopedValue.where(KEY, value).run(task). It previewed from Java 21 and is final in Java 25 (JEP 506). The binding ends with the call, so there's no remove to forget and no leak. Called code can't change it, so data flow is one-way, and a nested where rebinding only lasts for that inner call. Keep ThreadLocal for real per-thread caching or code that needs to mutate its value. The older signatures such as callWhere differ from the final API, so check which version an example targets.
Core 2, max 4, ArrayBlockingQueue of 2, tasks that never finish quickly. What happens to tasks 1 to 7?

Verified: tasks 1 and 2 start core threads, 3 and 4 go in the queue, 5 and 6 start extra threads (pool size 4), and 7 is rejected with RejectedExecutionException under the default policy. Threads only grow past core after the queue is full. Tasks 5 and 6 begin running before 3 and 4, which still sit in the queue.
Core 10, max 50, with new LinkedBlockingQueue(). How many threads can you get?

Only 10. The queue is effectively unbounded, so offer always succeeds and the "start extra worker" step is never reached. Tested with core 2, max 10: 100 blocked tasks gave 2 threads and 98 queued. The maximumPoolSize setting looks like protection, but it does nothing, and the failure mode becomes a growing queue, rising latency and eventually out-of-memory. Use a bounded queue.
Why is it recommended not to use the Executors factory methods in production?

They hide unbounded resources. newFixedThreadPool and newSingleThreadExecutor have an unbounded queue, so overload becomes a memory problem and queued tasks wait with no limit. newCachedThreadPool has an effectively unlimited thread count, so a burst of slow calls can create thousands of threads. They also give default thread names and offer no rejection path. Construct ThreadPoolExecutor directly, with a bounded queue, a named ThreadFactory and a chosen rejection policy, so that overload behaviour is a decision you made. They're fine for tools and tests with known, small workloads.
execute() vs submit(): how do exceptions differ?

execute takes a Runnable and returns nothing. An exception escapes, reaches the thread's uncaught exception handler and kills that worker, which the pool replaces. submit wraps the task in a FutureTask. The exception is stored and only appears as ExecutionException when someone calls get().
Verified: submit printed nothing until get() threw ExecutionException with cause IllegalStateException: from submit, while execute reached the handler at once. So a submit whose future is ignored fails silently. Catch and log inside the task, or override afterExecute.
shutdown() vs shutdownNow() vs close()?

- shutdown(): rejects new tasks, finishes queued and running ones, and returns immediately.
- shutdownNow(): rejects new tasks, removes queued tasks and returns them as a list, and interrupts running workers. Tasks that ignore interruption keep going.
- awaitTermination: blocks until finished or timeout. It returns false on timeout. It doesn't shut anything down itself.
- close() (Java 19): shutdown plus waiting, with shutdownNow if the waiting thread is interrupted. Lets you use try-with-resources.
Scenario: an API averages 100 ms per request, with 10 ms CPU and 90 ms waiting on the database, on 8 cores, at 500 requests per second. Size the thread pool.

Little's law: 500 × 0.1 s = 50 concurrent requests on average. Goetz: 8 × (1 + 90/10) = 80 threads at full CPU. Total CPU demand is 500 × 10 ms = 5 cores' worth, so 8 cores are enough.
So start around 60 to 80 threads, with a bounded queue short enough that its wait is acceptable, for example 100 tasks, which adds about 0.2 s of waiting at that rate. Then check the database: if each request holds a connection for most of the 90 ms, you need about 45 connections, so a pool of 10 would be the true bottleneck. Finally, load test and watch p99 latency, because averages hide spikes.
Which rejection policy would you choose for (a) a payment API, (b) a metrics pipeline, (c) a batch importer?

- (a) Payment API: AbortPolicy. Fail fast, return 503 with Retry-After, and let the client retry. Dropping money events silently is unacceptable, and running on the request thread just hides the overload.
- (b) Metrics: DiscardPolicy or DiscardOldestPolicy plus a dropped-event counter. Recent data is what matters.
- (c) Batch importer: CallerRunsPolicy. The reading thread slows down to match the workers, which gives back-pressure for free.
scheduleAtFixedRate vs scheduleWithFixedDelay? What if a run throws?

Fixed rate measures from start to start, and fixed delay measures from the end of one run to the start of the next. If a run overruns the period with fixed rate, the next one starts late. Runs of one task never overlap.
An exception cancels all future runs with no log. Tested with a 10 ms period and a task that throws on run 3: after 200 ms it had run exactly 3 times, isDone() was true, and get() threw ExecutionException. Wrap the body in try/catch for Exception, and log it.
How does ForkJoinPool differ from ThreadPoolExecutor?

| ThreadPoolExecutor | ForkJoinPool
Queue | One shared queue | A deque per worker plus submission queues
Balancing | Workers take from the shared queue | Work stealing
Best for | Independent tasks, often blocking | Recursive, short, non-blocking tasks
Waiting for subtasks | A blocked worker is lost | join() helps by running other tasks
Contention | Shared queue is a hot spot with many tiny tasks | Low, because mostly local
thenApply vs thenCompose vs thenCombine?
Which thread runs the callback in thenApply? In thenApplyAsync?

For thenApply, it depends on timing. If the stage is complete when you attach the callback, the attaching thread runs it. If not, the thread that later completes the stage runs it. completedFuture(1).thenRun(printThreadName) printed main; in a pending chain the same code would run on a pool thread, so don't rely on one or the other.
thenApplyAsync(fn) always submits to the common pool (it printed a ForkJoinPool name) and thenApplyAsync(fn, executor) to that executor. A slow non-async callback can block the thread of the task that completed it, so use the async variant for anything heavy.
exceptionally vs handle vs whenComplete?

exceptionally runs only on failure and returns a replacement value. handle always runs, receives the value and the exception, and its return becomes the new result, so it can recover. whenComplete always runs but can't change the outcome: the original value or exception passes through.
Verified: handle((v, e) -> e == null ? v : -1) gave -1. whenComplete saw the failure, and join() still threw CompletionException. Note that if the whenComplete action itself throws while the stage had succeeded, the result becomes that new exception.
Output? What does the exception handler receive in each of these?
What does CompletableFuture.allOf(a, b).join() return? Does it stop on the first failure?

It returns null, because it's a CompletableFuture<Void> (verified). Read the values afterward with a.join(), which won't block by then. It doesn't fail fast either: it completes only after all inputs finish, then reports a failure. In a test, a failed future and a 300 ms task together took the full 300 ms.
Does orTimeout or cancel(true) stop a running CompletableFuture task?

No. A CompletableFuture doesn't know which thread is doing its work. cancel just completes it with CancellationException, and mayInterruptIfRunning is ignored. orTimeout completes it with TimeoutException. In both cases the task continues, holding its thread and possibly its side effects. To really stop work, keep the Future from an ExecutorService.submit and call cancel(true) on it, have the task check a flag, or use structured concurrency. Client-level timeouts on the HTTP or JDBC call are also needed, since those are what actually free the thread.
Virtual threads: what are they, and when should you not use them?

JVM-managed threads, final in Java 21. They mount on a small set of carrier platform threads while running and unmount to the heap when blocked, so you can write simple blocking code and still handle a huge number of concurrent tasks.
Avoid them, or get no gain, for:
- CPU-bound work: use a pool sized to the cores, or parallel streams.
- Workloads with few concurrent tasks: nothing to gain.
- Code relying on heavy ThreadLocal caches per thread: memory grows with task count.
- Java 21 to 23 code with long I/O inside synchronized, including in libraries: pinning, which is fixed in Java 24.
- Unbounded access to a limited resource: add a semaphore or pool limit.
What is pinning? What did JEP 491 change, and what's left?

Pinning means a virtual thread can't unmount, so when it blocks it holds its carrier too. On Java 21 to 23 this happens while inside synchronized, and during native code. Because the scheduler has few carriers, a handful of pinned threads can stall a whole server. Symptoms include requests hanging while CPU sits idle.
JEP 491 (Java 24) lets virtual threads acquire, hold and release monitors independently of their carrier, so they can unmount inside synchronized and in Object.wait(). Pinning remains for native frames (JNI or foreign function calls on the stack) and class initialization. Detect it with the JFR event jdk.VirtualThreadPinned.
Output? Print isDaemon, getPriority and isVirtual for a virtual thread, then call setDaemon(false) and setPriority(10).
You move to virtual threads and the database pool starts timing out. Why? And should you put virtual threads in a pool to fix it?

The old fixed thread pool was acting as an accidental limit: at most 200 requests could reach the database. With unlimited virtual threads, thousands pile onto a connection pool of 20. Many wait, and they time out.
Don't pool virtual threads. Limit the actual resource: size the connection pool properly and let its queue and timeout do the work, or guard the call with a Semaphore. Decide what to do when overloaded, too, since rejecting early is usually better than queuing without limit.
How is structured concurrency better than CompletableFuture for fan-out, and can you use it in production?

With CompletableFuture, a failing branch doesn't cancel its siblings, cancellation doesn't reach running tasks, and threads have no parent-child relation. Structured concurrency ties subtasks to a scope: on failure the others are cancelled by interruption, the block doesn't exit until they've finished, and you write plain blocking code with ordinary try/catch.
It's still a preview API on Java 25, and it changed form across releases, so production use means enabling preview features and accepting API changes. For stable code today, use CompletableFuture or an executor with explicit cancellation.
A service hangs with low CPU in production. Walk through your diagnosis.

- Take three thread dumps a few seconds apart, before restarting anything.
- Look for "Found one Java-level deadlock" at the end of the dump.
- Look for many threads BLOCKED on one address. Then find who holds it and what it's waiting on.
- Look for workers stuck in socketRead, HikariPool.getConnection or similar. Slow downstream calls and exhausted connection pools are the most common real cause, and the fix is usually timeouts.
- Check whether all pool threads wait on Future.get for tasks in the same pool (thread-starvation deadlock).
- Check GC logs too: long pauses also look like a hang.
- On virtual threads, get a dump with jcmd Thread.dump_to_file, and check for pinning on Java 21 to 23.
Show how a single-thread executor can deadlock with no locks.
Livelock vs starvation, with examples?

Livelock: threads are active but make no progress, like two people in a corridor who keep stepping aside the same way. In code, two threads using tryLock on two locks each fail, release and retry in lockstep. Random backoff fixes it.
Starvation: others progress but a thread doesn't. A low-priority task behind a steady flow in a priority queue, a writer behind constant readers, or a reader in a non-fair lock with long holders. Fix with fair policies, aging priorities or separate pools.
What is false sharing and how would you detect it?

Independent variables that share a cache line cause cores to invalidate each other's cache copies on each write. Logically unrelated threads slow each other down, with correct results but poor scaling.
Clues: throughput falling as threads are added to work that shares no data, with counters or per-thread slots in one array or object. Confirm with hardware counters (for example perf c2c on Linux) or by adding padding and measuring with JMH. Fix by separating the data, padding, or per-thread state merged later, which is what LongAdder does.
Design: compute an expensive value once per key, even with many concurrent callers.
Design: process events concurrently but keep order per customer.
Design: gracefully stop a queue consumer so no accepted message is lost.

- Stop accepting new work: close the source or set a flag.
- Call pool.shutdown(), so queued tasks still run.
- Wait with awaitTermination for a bounded time, shorter than the platform's kill timeout (Kubernetes defaults to 30 s).
- If time runs out, call shutdownNow(), and save the returned tasks, or leave them unacknowledged so that the broker redelivers them.
- Consumers should end with the interrupt protocol, and acknowledge only after processing finishes.
Run this from a shutdown hook, or let Spring's lifecycle do it (server.shutdown=graceful in Spring Boot). Delivery is usually at-least-once, so handlers must be idempotent.
Why shouldn't you start a thread in a constructor?

It lets this escape before construction finishes. The new thread can see default field values, and final-field guarantees don't apply yet, because the constructor hasn't completed. Subclass constructors won't have run either, so an overridden method called by the thread can act on an uninitialized subclass. Instead, use a private constructor plus a static factory method that creates the object, then starts the thread.
Why is SimpleDateFormat a classic concurrency bug?

It keeps parsing state in a mutable Calendar field. A shared static instance gives wrong dates, or exceptions such as NumberFormatException, under load, usually only in production. Fixes, best first: use the immutable DateTimeFormatter, create a new instance per use, or wrap it in a ThreadLocal.
Your synchronized booking method prevents double bookings locally, but in production with 3 pods two users booked the same seat. Why, and how do you fix it?

A Java lock only protects threads in one JVM; each pod has its own monitor, so both requests entered the critical section. Move the guarantee to the shared store: a unique constraint on (show_id, seat_no), an atomic conditional UPDATE … WHERE status = 'FREE' checking the row count, optimistic locking with @Version, or SELECT … FOR UPDATE. Use a distributed lock only if no DB-level guarantee fits.
💡 Interviewers like hearing "the database is the source of truth for the invariant, so the database should enforce it".
How do you avoid one global lock when updates for different keys are independent?

Lock per key. The easy route is ConcurrentHashMap.compute(key, …), which is atomic per key. For arbitrary critical sections, use lock striping: a fixed array of locks indexed by floorMod(key.hashCode(), n). It bounds memory and avoids the leak of a never-cleaned Map<Key, Lock>. When two keys are needed, lock stripes in a consistent order.
You doubled the thread pool from 50 to 100 and throughput did not improve. Why?

Something serial is the bottleneck (Amdahl's law): a shared lock, a hot DB row, a DB connection pool of 20, a rate-limited downstream API, or CPU saturation. Extra threads just queue on that resource and add context switching and memory. Measure where threads wait (thread dump, JFR lock profiling, pool metrics like Hikari pending connections) and fix the constraint: raise the downstream limit, partition the hot data, batch, or cache.
Which concurrent collection would you pick for: a read-mostly listener list, a shared cache, a sorted concurrent index, a work queue?

- Read-mostly listeners: CopyOnWriteArrayList (iteration never throws, writes copy the array).
- Shared cache/map: ConcurrentHashMap (or Caffeine when you need eviction).
- Sorted concurrent map/set: ConcurrentSkipListMap/Set.
- Producer–consumer: a bounded ArrayBlockingQueue or LinkedBlockingQueue(capacity) for back-pressure; ConcurrentLinkedQueue if you never need to block.
Avoid Collections.synchronizedX in new code: compound actions and iteration still need external locking.
Is it safe to use @Transactional with a Java lock, e.g. lock, then call a transactional method, then unlock?

Often not. If the lock is acquired inside the transactional method, the unlock happens before the proxy commits, so a second thread can enter and read the old, uncommitted state. The lock must wrap the whole transaction (acquire before the transactional call, release after it returns), and even then it only works on one instance. Prefer a DB-level guarantee (constraint, conditional update, row lock).
volatile vs synchronized vs AtomicInteger: what does each one guarantee?

| volatile | synchronized | AtomicInteger
Visibility of writes | Yes | Yes (on unlock / lock of the same monitor) | Yes (volatile semantics)
Atomic count++ | No | Yes | Yes (incrementAndGet, CAS)
Mutual exclusion | No | Yes | No (lock-free retry)
Invariant over several fields | No | Yes | No, one variable only
Can block a thread | No | Yes | No
volatile boolean running = true;        // fine: one writer sets a flag
private final AtomicInteger hits = new AtomicInteger();
hits.incrementAndGet();                 // fine: single counter
synchronized void transfer(Account a, Account b, int x) { a.debit(x); b.credit(x); } // two fields together
Rule of thumb: volatile for a flag or a safely published reference, an atomic for one counter or one reference updated with CAS, a lock when two or more values must change together.
ConcurrentHashMap vs Collections.synchronizedMap vs Hashtable?

| ConcurrentHashMap | synchronizedMap(new HashMap()) | Hashtable
Locking | Lock-free reads; writes use CAS or lock one bin | One mutex for every call | Every method synchronized on the table
Readers block writers? | No | Yes | Yes
Iteration while others write | Weakly consistent, never throws CME | Fail-fast; you must hold the lock while iterating | Fail-fast iterators; you must lock
null keys / values | Not allowed | Allowed (like HashMap) | Not allowed
Status | The default choice | For wrapping an existing map | Legacy, avoid
Rule of thumb: use ConcurrentHashMap and its atomic methods (computeIfAbsent, merge) instead of get-then-put. The other two serialize every access through one lock.
wait/notify vs Lock with Condition vs BlockingQueue for producer-consumer?

| wait / notify | Lock + Condition | BlockingQueue
Wait sets per lock | One | As many as you create (notFull, notEmpty) | Hidden inside
Wake-up precision | notifyAll usually needed | signal() on the right condition | Handled for you
Timeouts | wait(ms) | await(time, unit), awaitNanos | offer/poll(time, unit)
Loop for spurious wakeups | You write it | You write it | Not needed
Code you write | Most | Medium | Least (put / take)
Rule of thumb: in real code use a BlockingQueue; ArrayBlockingQueue is itself built on one ReentrantLock and two Conditions. Write wait/notify or Condition code only when an interviewer asks for it.
Parallel stream vs your own ExecutorService vs CompletableFuture: which for parallel work?

| parallelStream() | ExecutorService | CompletableFuture
Threads used | Common ForkJoinPool (cores - 1) plus the caller | The pool you size and name | Common pool, unless you pass an executor
Good for | CPU-bound work on a large, splittable collection | Independent tasks, blocking I/O, isolation | Chaining and combining async steps
Blocking I/O inside | Bad: starves every user of the common pool | Fine with a sized pool or virtual threads | Fine if you pass your own executor
Error handling | First exception is rethrown to the caller | Future.get() throws ExecutionException | exceptionally, handle
Ordering | Kept for ordered sources unless you use forEach | Your choice | Your choice
Rule of thumb: parallel streams only for pure CPU work on big data. For calls to databases or services, use your own executor (or virtual threads) and compose with CompletableFuture, always passing that executor.
